bw: Pressure of blood against the capillary wall
Drives fluid out into the tissues
tp: CHP is the same as capillary blood pressure, about 35 mm Hg at the arterial end falling to about 18 mm Hg at the venous end.

ww.Blood colloid osmotic pressure: BCOP draws fluid back into the capillary rather than pushing it out.
ww.Interstitial fluid osmotic pressure: This is always very low because interstitial fluid has few proteins.

evidence: CHP is the force that drives fluid out of capillaries and into the tissues.

bw: Pressure from plasma proteins
Draws water back into the capillary
tp: BCOP stays fairly constant at about 25 mm Hg along the capillary because the proteins cannot cross the capillary wall.

ww.Capillary hydrostatic pressure: CHP pushes fluid out of the capillary.
ww.Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure: IFHP opposes filtration and rises as fluid enters the tissue.

evidence: The pressure created by the concentration of colloidal proteins in the blood is called the blood colloidal osmotic pressure (BCOP).

bw: Fluid moves from tissues back into the capillary
Driven by osmotic pressure
tp: Reabsorption happens when NFP is negative, mainly near the venous end of the capillary.

ww.Filtration: Filtration is movement of fluid out of the capillary.
ww.Endocytosis: Endocytosis moves large proteins in vesicles, not bulk fluid.

evidence: In contrast, the movement of fluid from an area of higher pressure in the tissues into an area of lower pressure in the capillaries is reabsorption.

bw: Fluid moves out of the capillary into the interstitial fluid
Driven by hydrostatic pressure
tp: Filtration dominates at the arterial end, where CHP is higher than BCOP.

ww.Reabsorption: Reabsorption moves fluid from the tissues into the capillary.
ww.Endocytosis: Endocytosis is vesicle transport of large proteins.

bw: CHP minus BCOP
Net pressure driving fluid out of the capillary
tp: When reabsorption is occurring, NFP is a negative number.

ww.Pulse pressure: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic arterial pressure.
ww.Mean arterial pressure: MAP is the average arterial driving pressure.

evidence: The net filtration pressure (NFP) represents the interaction of the hydrostatic and osmotic pressures, driving fluid out of the capillary.

bw: Arterial end of the capillary
CHP 35 mm Hg minus BCOP 25 mm Hg
tp: The positive NFP drives a net movement of fluid out of the capillary at the arterial end.

ww.About 0 mm Hg: NFP is zero near the middle of the capillary, where CHP equals BCOP.
ww.About −7 mm Hg: That is the NFP at the venous end, where reabsorption occurs.

evidence: Close to the arterial end of the capillary, it is approximately 10 mm Hg, because the CHP of 35 mm Hg minus the BCOP of 25 mm Hg equals 10 mm Hg.

bw: Venous end of the capillary
CHP has fallen to about 18 mm Hg
tp: BCOP stays at 25 mm Hg, so water is drawn into the capillary (reabsorption).

ww.About +10 mm Hg: That is the NFP at the arterial end.
ww.About 0 mm Hg: NFP is zero near the middle of the capillary.

evidence: Another way of expressing this is to say that at the venous end of the capillary, there is an NFP of −7 mm Hg.

bw: Key contributors to osmotic pressure in blood
Form a colloid, not a true solution
tp: The formed elements of the blood do not contribute to the osmotic concentration gradients.

ww.Erythrocytes: The source states formed elements do not contribute to osmotic gradients.
ww.Sodium ions: Solute concentrations are similar across the wall and have no significant effect on osmosis.

evidence: Rather, it is the plasma proteins that play the key role.

bw: Excess filtered fluid returned to the blood
Recycled blood plasma
tp: Lymphatic capillaries pick up the excess and return it to the blood.

ww.Serum: Serum is plasma without clotting factors, not recovered tissue fluid.
ww.Cerebrospinal fluid: CSF bathes the brain and spinal cord.

evidence: Lymph may be thought of as recycled blood plasma.

bw: Fluid filtered by capillaries per day
Only 20.4 liters are reabsorbed
tp: The 3.6 liter surplus is picked up by lymphatic capillaries.

ww.About 4 liters: That is roughly the surplus, not the total filtered.
ww.About 60 liters: The source gives about 24 liters filtered per day.

evidence: Approximately 24 liters per day are filtered, whereas 20.4 liters are reabsorbed.

bw: Lymphatic vessels finally drain into these veins in the neck
tp: Thin-walled lymphatic vessels have many valves that keep flow one-way.

ww.Pulmonary veins: Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

evidence: These extremely thin-walled vessels have copious numbers of valves that ensure unidirectional flow through ever-larger lymphatic vessels that eventually drain into the subclavian veins in the neck.

bw: Capillary-like gaps large enough for plasma proteins to pass
tp: Fenestrated capillaries have pores that allow larger molecules through.

ww.Fenestrated capillaries: Their pores pass larger molecules, but the source gives the great gaps to sinusoids.
ww.Lymphatic capillaries: Lymphatic capillaries return fluid to the blood and are not described as the gaps in question.

evidence: Larger molecules can pass through the pores of fenestrated capillaries, and even large plasma proteins can pass through the great gaps in the sinusoids.

bw: Gases and lipid-soluble molecules
Cross the endothelial cell membrane directly
tp: Water moves by osmosis, and larger plasma proteins may cross in vesicles.

ww.Facilitated diffusion: This uses transporters, as for glucose, amino acids and ions.
ww.Endocytosis: Endocytosis moves some large proteins in vesicles.

evidence: Small molecules, such as gases, lipids, and lipid-soluble molecules, can diffuse directly through the membranes of the endothelial cells of the capillary wall.

bw: Glucose, amino acids and ions crossing the capillary membrane
Use transporters in specific channels
tp: Glucose, ions and larger molecules may also leave the blood through intercellular clefts.

ww.Simple diffusion: Gases and lipid-soluble molecules diffuse directly through the membrane.
ww.Bulk flow: Bulk flow is the pressure-driven mass movement of fluid, not a transporter process.

evidence: Glucose, amino acids, and ions—including sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride—use transporters to move through specific channels in the membrane by facilitated diffusion.
